title: Counting clicks that arrive late
teaches: Event time and processing time, windows and watermarks, exactly-once effects by deduplication, and sketches for heavy hitters

blocks.text: An advertiser on Google's search pages pays when someone clicks the ad, so every click is money. The click itself is logged by one server, and the search that showed the ad was logged earlier by another, perhaps in another datacentre; to bill the click, the two records have to be found and joined. In June 2013, at the SIGMOD conference in New York, Rajagopal Ananthanarayanan and his colleagues described Photon, the system that did that join for Google's advertising, continuously, across datacentres, so advertisers could see their spending within seconds instead of the next day.

Photon's paper puts its load at millions of events a minute with an end-to-end delay of under ten seconds on average.[^photon] The numbers are not what made it hard. What made it hard is what the paper calls its requirements, set out before any design: no click may be billed twice, no click may be lost, and the system must keep going if a whole datacentre fails.

Photon's builders worked in an order worth copying: **define what a correct answer is** before building the pipeline. For a count of clicks a minute, that means three answers written down first. Which minute does a click belong to: the one in which it happened, or the one in which the pipeline saw it? When is a minute's count finished, given that some clicks will arrive later? And what happens to a click that arrives twice? Every streaming system makes these choices; the ones that do not make them on purpose make them by accident.

Each event has two times. Its **event time** is when it happened: when the finger touched the ad. Its **processing time** is when the pipeline handled it. The gap between them is never zero and often large. Logs are shipped in batches every few seconds; a phone in a tunnel holds its events until it is back online, minutes or hours later; a datacentre that was cut off for twenty minutes sends twenty minutes of events all at once when it comes back.

A stream is counted in **windows**, slices of time each with its own count. **Fixed** windows (also called tumbling) cut time into equal pieces, one per minute. **Sliding** windows overlap: the last five minutes, recomputed every minute. **Session** windows follow activity: one per burst of a user's actions, ending after, say, 30 minutes of silence. Any of them can be cut by either clock.

Cutting windows by processing time is simple, since the pipeline only needs its own clock, and it is the wrong choice for a bill. Suppose a datacentre's click logs are held up for twenty minutes and then drain in two. A count by processing time shows nothing for twenty minutes and then a burst ten times the normal rate, and an advertiser whose budget is spread over the hour sees it spent in two minutes of clicks that did not happen then. A count by event time puts every click back in the minute it happened. The price is that the pipeline can never be sure a minute is over.

By event time, the minute from 12:00 to 12:01 is not finished at 12:01, nor at 12:05, since a phone could still be in a tunnel with a click from 12:00:30. A pipeline has to decide when to answer anyway, and the tool for that is a **watermark**: the pipeline's running estimate of how far event time has got. A watermark of 12:01 means "I believe every event before 12:01 has now arrived". When the watermark passes a window's end, the window gives its answer. Tyler Akidau and his colleagues at Google described watermarks in MillWheel (VLDB 2013) and set out the whole vocabulary in the Dataflow Model paper (VLDB 2015), which Apache Beam and Apache Flink follow.[^watermark]

A watermark is usually a guess, built from what the sources report about their oldest unsent data or, at simplest, from a rule such as "nothing is more than 20 seconds late". When it is wrong, an event arrives after its window has answered. That is a **late** event, and the pipeline must decide what to do with it: drop it, or send a revised answer for the window. The figure plots each click by when it happened (across) and when it arrived (up). A click on the diagonal, where the two times are equal, arrived the instant it happened; the higher above the diagonal, the later it arrived. The brown line is the watermark rule, drawn as far above the diagonal as the watermark waits, and a click above that line is late.

blocks.task: Find settings that end with every minute's count right, and play the clock to the end

blocks.text: With a 20-second watermark and late clicks dropped, each minute is answered 20 seconds after it ends, and four of the five are short by a click. Raising the wait to four minutes catches every click in the first answer, and each answer comes four minutes late. Keeping the short wait and revising gets both: a fast first answer and a correct final one, at the cost that whatever reads the counts must accept a number changing. Most real pipelines do that, with a limit called the **allowed lateness**, say an hour or a day; past it, the window's state is thrown away and anything later is dropped or sent to a separate correction job, because no pipeline can keep every window open for ever. Set it from the data: measure how late events really arrive, and choose a lateness that covers nearly all of them, say 99.99%, leaving the rest to the correction job.

A billing pipeline revises; a dashboard of clicks a minute may do better to drop and say so; an alert that pages someone at night wants the first answer fast and will never use a revision. These are choices about what the reader of the number needs, which is why they come before the design.

Lesson 16 ended with a log that delivers **at least once**: a consumer that crashes is replaced by one that starts from the last committed offset and reads some events again. Below the log, the same thing happens on the network. A phone that sends a click and hears no acknowledgement cannot tell whether the click was lost or only the acknowledgement was, so it sends again, and sometimes the log holds two copies. Lesson 22 shows that no protocol over an unreliable network can avoid this: exactly-once *delivery* is impossible.

What can be had is an **exactly-once effect**: the count goes up once per click, however many times the click is delivered. There are two ways. One makes the effect itself safe to repeat, **idempotent**, like setting a value instead of adding to it: "click 42 was on ad 7" written to a table keyed by click ID can be written ten times with one result. The other keeps a record of the IDs already counted and drops any repeat. Both need every event to carry a unique ID from its source, chosen once, before the first send.

Photon took the second way, at the scale of datacentres. It ran the whole pipeline in two or more datacentres at once, each reading every click, so that losing one cost nothing. Before counting a click, a joiner had to claim the click's ID in the **IdRegistry**, a table of IDs counted in the last few days, replicated across datacentres with Paxos (lesson 11). Whichever joiner claimed first counted the click; every other claim was refused. Sizing such a registry is arithmetic: IDs a day times days kept. At 50,000 clicks a second that is 4.3 billion IDs a day, and three days of 16-byte IDs is about 200 GB before replication.

blocks.caption: One click sent twice, read by joiners in two datacentres. Times are illustrative.
blocks.task: Play it with no registry, then with the ID registry

blocks.text: A Paxos round across datacentres takes tens of milliseconds. A group committing one claim per round, one round after another, would manage a few dozen claims a second, while clicks arrive by the tens of thousands a second. Photon's registry servers gathered claims arriving close together and committed them in one round, and the registry was split by ID across many such groups, so the round trip was shared by many clicks. There remains one gap: a joiner that claims an ID and crashes before writing its output has counted nothing, and the ID is taken. Photon closed it with a separate process that finds such clicks and sends them again. So its count was never too high, could be briefly too low, and became exact soon after.[^gap]

Some questions a stream is asked have answers too big to keep exactly. "Which hundred pages were viewed most today?" needs a count for every page that might be among them, which over billions of pages is billions of counters. "How many different people visited?" needs the set of everyone seen. A **sketch** answers such questions approximately in a fixed amount of memory, with an error bound that can be chosen in advance.

The **count-min sketch** (Graham Cormode and S. Muthukrishnan, 2005) is a small table of counters: *d* rows of *w* each, and a different hash function for each row. Its size is set by two numbers chosen in advance: ε, the largest error allowed, as a share of all items counted, and δ, the chance of exceeding it. To count an item, add one to the counter its hash picks in every row. To estimate an item's count, look at its *d* counters and take the smallest. Each counter is shared by every item that hashes to it, so every counter is at least the item's true count, and the smallest is the one least crowded by other items. The estimate can be too high, never too low.

blocks.caption: A count-min sketch of 200,000 views of 50,000 pages whose popularity falls off steeply, as real pages' does. Made-up data. The two sliders set the counters a row, w, and the rows, d; the sketch holds w × d counters.
blocks.task: Find a sketch of at most 2,500 counters in all (w × d) that names the top ten pages correctly

blocks.text: The error depends on the width and the total count, not on how many distinct items there are. With *w* = *e*/ε counters a row (*e* ≈ 2.718) and *d* = ln(1/δ) rows, an estimate is at most ε times the total too high, except with chance δ. For error under 0.1% of all views, *w* is about 2,700; for δ = 1%, ln(100) ≈ 4.6, so five rows: 13,600 counters, about 54 KB, whether there are a thousand pages or a billion. A sketch also merges: two machines' sketches with the same hashes add counter by counter, so each machine can sketch its share of the stream and a final step sums them. To find the top pages, keep a small heap of the current leaders beside the sketch, and check each arriving page's estimate against the smallest in it.

Distinct counts have their own sketch, **HyperLogLog** (Philippe Flajolet and colleagues, 2007). It hashes each item, uses the first 11 bits of the hash to choose one of 2,048 buckets, and keeps in each bucket a 6-bit register holding the longest run of leading zero bits seen in the rest of the hash. Long runs are rare, so the longest runs say roughly how many distinct items went by. 2,048 registers of 6 bits is 1.5 KB, and it counts billions of distinct items to within about 2%, and HyperLogLogs merge as count-min sketches do.[^hll]

Early streaming systems were trusted for speed and not for accuracy, so many companies ran two pipelines over the same data: a stream for answers within seconds, and a nightly batch job (lesson 8's MapReduce) whose results replaced the stream's when they arrived. Nathan Marz called this the **lambda architecture**. It works, and it means writing every piece of logic twice, in two systems, and keeping them in agreement.

In 2014 Jay Kreps argued for one pipeline instead, sometimes called the **kappa architecture**. Keep the input in a log with long retention (lesson 16), and when the logic changes or a bug is fixed, start a second copy of the same streaming job from the oldest offset, let it catch up, and switch readers over to its output. Event-time windows, watermarks and deduplication by ID are what make that work: replaying last week through the stream gives the same counts as the live run's final answers, because the answer depends on when clicks happened, not when they were read. The one difference is clicks that arrived later than the allowed lateness: the live run dropped them, and a replay of the stored log sees them in time, so the replay is the more complete of the two.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on windows, watermarks and counting
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A datacentre's click logs are held up for twenty minutes, then drain in two. Why should a billing pipeline count clicks by event time rather than processing time?
choices: By processing time the twenty minutes' clicks all land in two minutes, a burst that never happened, and the quiet minutes show none
By processing time the held-up clicks are dropped as duplicates, because they arrive with timestamps the pipeline has already passed
By event time the pipeline needs no watermark at all, because each click already carries the minute it belongs to
items.why: Processing time records when the pipeline saw a click. Event time puts each click in the minute it happened, at the cost of having to decide when a minute is complete, which is what a watermark is for.

items.ask: What does a watermark of 12:01 claim?
choices: That the pipeline's own clock reads 12:01
That the pipeline estimates every event from before 12:01 has arrived, so windows ending by then can answer
That every event from before 12:01 is certain to have arrived, so any that comes later must be a duplicate
items.why: A watermark is an estimate of progress in event time. It is usually a heuristic and can be wrong, which is why late events and revisions exist.

items.ask: A pipeline answers each minute 20 seconds after it ends and drops late clicks; its counts are often a little low. Which change gives fast answers that end up exact for every click arriving within an hour?
choices: Count by processing time instead, so that every click is counted in the minute it arrives and none can be late
Keep the 20-second watermark, and revise a minute's count when late clicks arrive, with an hour's allowed lateness
Raise the watermark's wait to an hour
items.why: Revisions keep the first answer fast and correct it later, at the cost that readers must accept a changed number. A long wait is exact but slow; processing time counts the wrong minute.

items.ask: A phone sends a click, gets no acknowledgement and sends it again. How does a pipeline make sure the advertiser is charged once?
choices: Turn off retries on the phone, so that each click can only ever be sent across the network a single time
Use a message log that guarantees exactly-once delivery, so the second copy is never handed to a consumer
Give each click a unique ID at the source and count only the first time each ID is claimed in a shared registry
items.why: Without retries clicks are lost, and exactly-once delivery over a lossy network is impossible. Deduplication by a unique ID, or an idempotent write keyed by it, gives an exactly-once effect.

items.ask: A count-min sketch estimates that a page was viewed 1,240 times. What can you say about its true count?
choices: It is at most 1,240, and probably close to it if the sketch is wide enough for the stream
It is at least 1,240, because other pages that share its counters can only have added to them
It is within 1% of 1,240 either way, whatever the width of the sketch and the size of the stream
items.why: Each counter holds the page's own views plus any other page's that hash there, so every counter, and the smallest of them, is at least the true count. The overestimate shrinks as the rows get wider.

items.ask: A service on 100 machines must report how many different people used it each day, out of about a billion. Which design fits?
choices: Each machine sends every user ID it sees to one central server, which keeps them all in a hash set
Each machine keeps a HyperLogLog of a few KB, and the hundred are merged into one at the end of the day
Each machine counts its own distinct users exactly, and the hundred counts are added together at the end
items.why: A billion IDs in one set is gigabytes on one machine. Adding per-machine counts counts anyone seen by two machines twice. HyperLogLogs merge without double counting, within about 2%.

items.ask: Photon claims a click's ID in its registry before writing the joined click. What is the risk in that order, and how is it handled?
choices: A joiner may claim and then crash, losing the click for a while, so a separate process finds such clicks and sends them again
Two joiners may both claim the same ID at once, so the click is billed twice until the advertiser asks for a refund
Claiming first adds a cross-datacentre round trip to every click, so Photon skips the registry for its cheapest ads
items.why: Every click is claimed in the registry, agreed by Paxos, which refuses a second claim, so double billing cannot happen. A crash between claim and output can lose a click, which is recovered later: never too high, eventually exact.

summary: **Define a correct answer first.** Decide which clock a window uses, when its answer is final, and what to do with late and repeated events before choosing machinery.
**Every event has two times.** Event time is when it happened, processing time when it was handled, and the gap can be seconds or hours.
**Bill by event time.** Windows by processing time turn a delayed backlog into a burst that never happened.
**A watermark estimates how far event time has got.** When it passes a window's end, the window answers; an event arriving after that is late.
**Waiting trades speed for completeness.** A short watermark with revisions gives fast first answers that end up right, up to an allowed lateness.
**Exactly-once delivery is impossible; exactly-once effects are not.** Give each event a unique ID at its source, then deduplicate or write idempotently.
**Photon claimed each click's ID in a Paxos-replicated registry.** Pipelines in several datacentres could all read every click, and only the first claim counted.
**Sketches answer big questions in small memory.** A count-min sketch overestimates by at most a chosen share of the total; HyperLogLog counts distinct items within about 2% in 1.5 KB.
**Replay can replace a second pipeline.** With event-time windows and deduplication, rerunning the log through the same stream job gives the same answer.

photon.title: Photon's numbers
photon.text: The paper gives peak rates in millions of joined events a minute and an average delay from click to joined output of under ten seconds. Its IdRegistry held the IDs of the last N days of clicks, so a click delivered again within that time could be recognised.

watermark.title: Perfect and heuristic watermarks
watermark.text: A source that knows its own data completely, such as a set of files with known contents, can give a perfect watermark that is never wrong. Most real sources, such as phones, can only give a heuristic one. The Dataflow paper also introduced triggers: rules for when a window answers (at the watermark, every minute until then, once per late event) and whether each answer replaces or adds to the last.

gap.title: Never too high
gap.text: The paper states its guarantee in three parts: at most once at any moment, nearly exact within seconds, and exactly once eventually. For billing, the order matters: charging a click late is acceptable, charging it twice is not.

hll.title: Coins and zeros
hll.text: Flip a coin until it first lands heads, and repeat. A run of k tails before the heads turns up about once in 2^k attempts, so if the longest run you saw was nine tails, you have probably made several hundred attempts. HyperLogLog treats each hashed item's leading zero bits as such a run, so each bucket's longest run suggests how many distinct items reached it, and it averages over the buckets so that one lucky run does not dominate. The error is about 1.04 divided by the square root of the number of buckets. Redis offers it as a built-in type with 16,384 buckets, 12 KB, for an error near 0.8%.
